content: Six weeks after a cesarean section, combined hormonal contraceptives can be initiated to reduce the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE). However, women with additional risk factors for VTE, beyond the postpartum period, should avoid using combined hormonal contraceptives (as per MMWR, July 7, 2011). Women with prediabetes or diabetes who are taking ethinyl estradiol/norethindrone should be closely monitored, and alternative contraceptive methods should be considered for those with uncontrolled dyslipidemia. Any significant changes in headache patterns should be evaluated, and therapy should be discontinued if necessary. Irregular bleeding or amenorrhea should also be assessed. Hormonal therapy should be discontinued before starting a combination drug regimen containing ombitasvir/paritaprevir/ritonavir, with or without dasabuvir. Hormonal therapy may be resumed approximately two weeks after completing the combination drug regimen. In women with hereditary angioedema, exogenous estrogens may trigger or worsen angioedema symptoms. Chloasma (skin discoloration) may occur during therapy, particularly in women with a history of chloasma gravidarum. Contraceptives are not needed during pregnancy and should be discontinued if pregnancy is confirmed. Extensive epidemiological studies have shown no increased risk of birth defects in women who used oral contraceptives before pregnancy. These studies also do not suggest teratogenic effects, particularly concerning cardiac anomalies and limb reduction defects, when oral contraceptives are inadvertently taken during early pregnancy. Oral contraceptives should not be used to induce withdrawal bleeding as a test for pregnancy, nor should they be used during pregnancy to treat threatened or habitual abortion. If a patient misses two consecutive periods, pregnancy should be ruled out before continuing oral contraceptive use. If the patient has not adhered to the prescribed schedule, pregnancy should be considered at the time of the first missed period, and oral contraceptives should be discontinued if pregnancy is confirmed. Small amounts of oral contraceptive steroids have been detected in the breast milk of nursing mothers, with a few reported adverse effects on infants, such as jaundice and breast enlargement. Additionally, oral contraceptives administered during the postpartum period may interfere with lactation by reducing the quantity and quality of breast milk. Nursing mothers should be advised to avoid oral contraceptives and use alternative forms of contraception until they have completely weaned their child. Ethinyl estradiol reduces the release of luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) from the hypothalamus and decreases gonadotropin release from the pituitary. It also increases the synthesis of DNA, RNA, and various proteins in target tissues. Norethindrone acetate, a progestin, inhibits gonadotropin secretion from the pituitary, prevents follicular maturation and ovulation, and stimulates mammary tissue growth. Ferrous fumarate is included to replenish iron stores. The peak plasma time for ethinyl estradiol is approximately 8 hours, while for norethindrone, it is 1-2 hours. Protein binding is 80% for ethinyl estradiol and 61% for norethindrone. Both components are metabolized in the liver, with ethinyl estradiol undergoing extensive first-pass metabolism. Ethinyl estradiol metabolites include estriol and estrone, while norethindrone metabolites include inactive sulfate and glucuronide forms. The half-life of norethindrone is 4-13 hours when taken orally. This information is provided for general educational purposes. Individual plans and formulary details may vary, and formulary information is subject to change. For the most current information, contact the applicable plan provider.
